title: Why People Stay
text:
It seems obvious that people stay in relationships because they are happy in them. The social psychologist Caryl Rusbult thought that explanation was incomplete. People sometimes leave satisfying relationships and stay in unsatisfying ones. She proposed an investment model of commitment with three ingredients: how satisfied a person is, how good their alternatives look, and how much they have already put into the relationship that they would lose by leaving.

To test it, Rusbult followed college students in dating relationships over about seven months. Every few weeks they completed questionnaires about the rewards and costs of the relationship, how attractive their alternatives were, what they had invested in it, such as time, shared friends, memories and effort, and how committed they felt. At the end she checked who had stayed together and who had broken up.

Commitment grew when satisfaction rose, but also when investments accumulated and when alternatives came to seem less appealing. Commitment, in turn, predicted whether people stayed together better than satisfaction alone did.

The model became one of the most widely tested in relationship science. Rusbult and colleagues later used it to help explain why some people remain in abusive relationships: few alternatives and heavy investments can hold a person in place.
lesson: Commitment is built from what you invest and what you choose not to chase, not only from how happy you feel today. Feed the relationship you want to keep.
source: Rusbult, C. E. (1983). A longitudinal test of the investment model: The development (and deterioration) of satisfaction and commitment in heterosexual involvements. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 45(1), 101-117.
